options.text: A client-side transition that keeps the shared layout mounted
options.why: Only `<Link>` (or `useRouter`) performs client-side transitions; a plain `<a>` does not.

options.text: A full page load, so client state in the layout is lost
options.why: A plain anchor triggers a normal browser navigation, which reloads the document.

options.text: The same as Blog, because Next.js upgrades all anchors
options.why: Next.js does not intercept plain `<a>` tags; you must use `<Link>` to get its behaviour.

options.text: Nothing, because `<a>` tags are blocked inside App Router layouts
options.why: Anchors work normally; they just navigate the way a regular website does.

explanation: `<Link>` extends `<a>` with prefetching and client-side transitions. A plain `<a href="/contact">` is not prefetched and makes the browser load a new document, so state, scroll position and the mounted layout are reset. The docs note this directly: an `a` tag triggers a full page navigation.

stem: In the App Router, `<Link>` prefetches routes as they enter the viewport while you run `next dev` as well as in a production build.

options.text: True
options.why: Prefetching is documented as production-only, so `next dev` will not show it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: automatic prefetching only runs in production builds.

explanation: The `<Link>` reference states that prefetching is only enabled in production. In development, routes are compiled and rendered on demand, so navigations may feel slower than they will in production. Test prefetching with `next build` and `next start`.

stem: Which import gives a Client Component in the App Router the router with `push`, `replace` and `refresh`?

options.text: `useRouter` from `'next/router'`, as in the Pages Router
options.why: That is the Pages Router hook; it is not the App Router router.

options.text: `import { router } from 'next/link'`
options.why: `next/link` exports the `Link` component and `useLinkStatus`, not a router object.

options.text: `import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'`
options.why: The App Router hooks (`useRouter`, `usePathname`, `useSearchParams`) live in `next/navigation`.

options.text: `import { useRouter } from 'react-dom'`
options.why: React has no router; routing is provided by Next.js.

explanation: In the App Router, `useRouter` comes from `next/navigation`. The old `next/router` hook belongs to the Pages Router: its `pathname` and `query` fields were replaced by `usePathname()` and `useSearchParams()`, and `router.events` was removed.

stem: A Server Component calls `redirect('/login')` from `next/navigation` before streaming starts (not in a Server Action). Which HTTP status code does the response use? Type the number.
explanation: `redirect()` responds with `307 Temporary Redirect`, which keeps the request method, unlike a `302` that browsers often turn into a GET. `permanentRedirect()` uses `308`. Inside Server Actions the rules differ: with JavaScript it performs a client-side navigation, and for progressive-enhancement form posts it sends a `303`.

stem: A Client Component renders on `/shop/shoes/nike?color=red` with the route `app/shop/[tag]/[item]/page.tsx`. Match each hook call to the value it returns.

options.text: `'/shop/shoes/nike'`
`'red'`
`{ tag: 'shoes', item: 'nike' }`
`'/shop/shoes/nike?color=red'`

explanation: `usePathname` returns the path only, without the query string. `useSearchParams` returns a read-only `URLSearchParams`, so `.get('color')` gives `'red'`. `useParams` returns the filled dynamic segments as an object. None of them returns the path with its query string attached.

stem: A Client Component calls `usePathname()` while the browser is on `/dashboard?v=2#stats`. What does it return?

options.text: `'/dashboard?v=2'`
options.why: The query string is not part of the pathname; read it with `useSearchParams`.

options.text: `'/dashboard'`
options.why: Only the path is returned, without the query string or hash.

options.text: `'dashboard'`
options.why: The pathname keeps its leading slash, for example `'/'` for the root.

options.text: `null`, because hashes aren't supported
options.why: In the App Router `usePathname` returns a string; the hash is simply ignored.

explanation: `usePathname` returns the current URL's pathname: `/dashboard?v=2` gives `'/dashboard'`. Search params come from `useSearchParams()`. The hash is client-only and never part of the pathname.

stem: A wizard step uses `<Link href="/checkout/payment" replace>Next</Link>`. What does the `replace` prop change?

options.text: It replaces the cached page with a freshly rendered copy from the server
options.why: `replace` is about browser history, not the client cache.

options.text: It reloads the whole document instead of transitioning
options.why: The navigation is still a client-side transition.

options.text: It skips prefetching for this one link
options.why: Prefetching is controlled by the `prefetch` prop.

options.text: It swaps the current history entry instead of adding one
options.why: Back then skips the replaced step and goes to the entry before it.

explanation: `replace` defaults to `false`, so `<Link>` normally pushes a new entry onto the history stack. With `replace`, the current entry is replaced, which is handy for flows where returning to an intermediate step via Back makes no sense. `router.replace()` does the same programmatically.

stem: Which of these can only be called from a Client Component, not from a Server Component? (Choose three.)

options.text: `useSearchParams()`
options.why: It is a Client Component hook; Server Component pages read the `searchParams` prop instead.

options.text: `usePathname()`
options.why: Reading the current URL from a Server Component is intentionally unsupported.

options.text: `useRouter()` from `next/navigation`
options.why: Programmatic navigation runs in the browser, so it is a Client Component hook.

options.text: `redirect()` from `next/navigation`
options.why: `redirect` works in Server Components, Route Handlers and Server Functions too.

options.text: `notFound()` from `next/navigation`
options.why: `notFound` is designed for Server Components, Server Functions and Route Handlers.

explanation: `useSearchParams`, `usePathname` and `useRouter` are hooks that read or drive browser state, so they need `'use client'`. `redirect()` and `notFound()` work by throwing a framework error, which is why they run in Server Components and Server Functions. `redirect` also runs during render in Client Components, but not in their event handlers.
reference: Next.js docs: useSearchParams, usePathname, redirect, notFound

stem: A statically prerendered page renders `<SearchBar />`, a Client Component that calls `useSearchParams()`, without any `<Suspense>` around it. Everything works in `next dev`. What happens in `next build`?

options.text: The build passes and the page is silently made dynamic
options.why: For a static page Next.js reports an error instead of switching it to dynamic.

options.text: The build passes, but `get()` returns `null` for every key
options.why: The hook is not left half-working; the build stops before that.

options.text: The build fails with a missing Suspense boundary error
options.why: A static page must wrap the `useSearchParams` caller in `<Suspense>`.

options.text: The build fails because hooks can't run during prerendering
options.why: Client Components do prerender; only the search-params part needs a boundary.

explanation: During prerendering the query string is unknown, so `useSearchParams` makes the tree up to the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary render on the client. With no boundary, a production build fails with "Missing Suspense boundary with useSearchParams". Development renders on demand, so the problem stays hidden there. Wrap the component in `<Suspense fallback={...}>`, or make the route dynamic deliberately, for example with `await connection()`.

stem: A dashboard page holds an open accordion in `useState` and the user has scrolled halfway down. A Client Component then calls `router.refresh()`. What happens?

options.text: The page reloads and the accordion closes
options.why: It is not a reload; unaffected client state is merged, not reset.

options.text: Server Components re-render; client and scroll state are kept
options.why: The new server payload is merged without losing unaffected client or browser state.

options.text: Only Client Components re-render; the server payload stays exactly as it was
options.why: It is the reverse: a new server request re-renders the Server Components.

options.text: All server-side caches for the route are purged
options.why: Refresh clears the client cache for the route, not the server-side cache.

explanation: `router.refresh()` makes a new request for the current route, re-runs data requests and re-renders Server Components. The client merges the new React Server Component payload without losing unaffected `useState` values or browser state such as scroll position. It clears the client cache for that route but leaves server-side caches alone; use `revalidatePath` or `revalidateTag` for those.

stem: Without Cache Components or Partial Prefetching, a `<Link href="/orders/42">` with the default `prefetch` scrolls into view. `/orders/[id]` is dynamic and its folder has a `loading.tsx`. What is prefetched?

options.text: The full route, including the order's data
options.why: Full prefetching is the default only for static routes, or with `prefetch={true}`.

options.text: Nothing, because dynamic routes are never prefetched
options.why: With a `loading.js` boundary, dynamic routes are partially prefetched.

options.text: Only the route's JavaScript chunks, with no React Server Component payload at all
options.why: The shared layouts and loading UI payload are prefetched as well.

options.text: The layouts down to the loading boundary, so the skeleton shows on click
options.why: Dynamic routes prefetch down to the nearest `loading.js`.

explanation: With the default `"auto"` (or `null`) setting, static routes are prefetched in full. Dynamic routes are prefetched down to the nearest `loading.js` boundary, or not at all if there is none. Here the layouts and the loading skeleton are ready ahead of time, so the click shows the skeleton instantly while the page streams in.
reference: Next.js docs: Prefetching (static vs dynamic routes)

stem: Which statements about the App Router `<Link prefetch>` prop are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `prefetch={false}` stops prefetching on viewport entry and on hover
options.why: In the App Router `false` disables both triggers.

options.text: `prefetch={true}` prefetches the full route even if it is dynamic
options.why: With `true` the full route is prefetched for static and dynamic routes alike.

options.text: `prefetch={false}` still prefetches when the user hovers
options.why: That is Pages Router behaviour; App Router `false` also disables hover.

options.text: `null` turns prefetching off, the same as `false`
options.why: `null` and `"auto"` mean the default behaviour.

options.text: The default prefetches dynamic routes in full
options.why: By default dynamic routes go only down to a `loading.js` boundary.

explanation: The App Router accepts `"auto"`/`null` (the default), `true` and `false`. The default prefetches static routes in full and dynamic routes down to their nearest loading boundary. `true` prefetches the full route either way. `false` never prefetches, on viewport entry or on hover. The Pages Router differs: there, `false` still prefetches on hover.

stem: A Server Component layout in `app/shop/layout.tsx` can read the current query string from a `searchParams` prop, just like a page can.

options.text: True
options.why: Only pages receive `searchParams`; layouts don't get that prop at all.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: shared layouts don't re-render on navigation, so they would show stale values.

explanation: Layouts persist across navigations and aren't re-rendered when only the page segment changes, so a `searchParams` prop on a layout would go stale. Read query params in the page, through its `searchParams` prop, or in a Client Component with `useSearchParams`, which re-renders on the client with the latest values.

stem:
After creating a post, this Server Action sends the user to the list, but the list doesn't show the new post. Why?

```ts
'use server'
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  await db.post.create({ data: { title: String(formData.get('title')) } })
  redirect('/posts')
  revalidatePath('/posts')
}
```

options.text: `revalidatePath` must receive the full URL, not a path
options.why: A route path such as `/posts` is the documented input.

options.text: `redirect` throws, so `revalidatePath` never runs
options.why: Nothing after `redirect()` executes; revalidate first, then redirect.

options.text: `redirect` must be returned, as `return redirect()`
options.why: `redirect` is typed `never`; a `return` is optional and changes nothing.

options.text: Server Actions can't revalidate paths they redirect to
options.why: Revalidating and then redirecting to the same path is the documented pattern.

explanation: `redirect()` throws a framework-handled control-flow exception, so any code after it is skipped. Here the cache for `/posts` is never invalidated, and the list renders stale data. Call `revalidatePath('/posts')` (or `revalidateTag`) first, then `redirect('/posts')`.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (redirect after a mutation)

stem: In Next.js 15 and later, what is the default value in seconds of `experimental.staleTimes.dynamic`, the client-cache lifetime for pages that are neither static nor fully prefetched? Type a number.
explanation: Since v15.0.0, `staleTimes.dynamic` defaults to 0 seconds, down from 30, so dynamic pages aren't reused from the client cache on a new navigation. `staleTimes.static` defaults to 5 minutes and covers static pages, `prefetch={true}` links and `router.prefetch()`. Back/forward navigation is a separate case and reuses cached entries regardless.

stem: In production, a user is on `/dashboard`, and a `<Link href="/dashboard/reports">` sits in the viewport. `/dashboard/reports` is dynamic and has its own `loading.tsx`, and both pages share `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`. Put these events in order.

options.text: The link enters the viewport and the route is prefetched down to its loading boundary
The user clicks the link
The shared dashboard layout stays mounted and the prefetched loading skeleton appears at once
The server renders the reports page and streams its payload to the client
The skeleton is swapped for the finished reports page

explanation: Prefetching happens before the click: for a dynamic route with `loading.tsx`, Next.js prefetches the layouts and the loading UI. On click, the client-side transition keeps the shared layout, shows the prefetched fallback immediately, and waits for the server to render and stream the page. The skeleton is then swapped for the finished content.
reference: Next.js docs: Linking and Navigating (streaming, client-side transitions)

stem: A Client Component calls `useSelectedLayoutSegment()`. Match each layout and URL to the value it returns.

options.text: `null`
`'analytics'`
`'dashboard'`

explanation: The hook returns the active segment exactly one level below the layout it is called from, or `null` if there isn't one. From the dashboard layout, `/dashboard` has no child segment, and `/dashboard/analytics/monthly` gives `'analytics'`. From the root layout the answer is `'dashboard'`. For a catch-all route the matched segments come back joined into one string, `'a/b/c'`.

stem: A Client Component calls `redirect('/thanks')` from `next/navigation` inside a button's `onClick` handler. What is the right fix?

options.text: Wrap the call in `startTransition` so React can schedule it
options.why: `redirect` isn't meant for event handlers; a transition doesn't change that.

options.text: Use `permanentRedirect` instead, which works in handlers
options.why: `permanentRedirect` has the same limits as `redirect`.

options.text: Use `useRouter().push('/thanks')` in the handler instead
options.why: `redirect` works during render, not in event handlers; use the router hook there.

options.text: Add `'use server'` at the top of the Client Component file
options.why: That would turn the module into Server Functions, not fix the handler.

explanation: The docs say `redirect` can be called in Client Components during the rendering process, but not in event handlers. For navigation in response to a click, use `useRouter().push()` or `replace()`. Another option is to submit to a Server Action that calls `redirect`, which then performs a client-side navigation.

stem: With the default `scroll` behaviour, a user who has scrolled far down a long page clicks a `<Link>` to another page under the same layout, and the new page's content is no longer in the viewport. What does Next.js do?

options.text: It always resets to the very top of the document
options.why: Next.js keeps the position if the new page is visible; it doesn't always reset.

options.text: It scrolls to the top of the first page element
options.why: If the new page is out of view, Next.js brings its first element into view.

options.text: It keeps the scroll position even though the page is out of view
options.why: The position is kept only while the new page is visible in the viewport.

options.text: It scrolls to the `<header>`, as the first sticky element
options.why: Sticky and fixed elements are skipped when finding the scroll target.

explanation: By default `<Link>` maintains the scroll position as long as the new page is visible in the viewport. If it isn't, Next.js scrolls to the top of the first page element, skipping sticky, fixed and non-visible elements. `scroll={false}` on `<Link>`, or `{ scroll: false }` on `router.push`/`replace`, turns this off. If content ends up behind a sticky header, use CSS `scroll-padding-top`.

stem: A `<form action={createPost}>` Server Action ends with `redirect('/posts')`. A user on a slow phone submits before the JavaScript bundle has loaded, so the browser does a native form POST. What does the server respond with?

options.text: A `307`, so the browser re-sends the POST to `/posts`
options.why: A `307` keeps the method; Server Action form posts deliberately avoid that.

options.text: A `308`, because Server Action redirects are permanent
options.why: `308` comes only from `permanentRedirect` outside this form-post case.

options.text: A `200` page that contains a client-side redirect meta tag for `/posts`
options.why: The meta-tag fallback is for redirects issued after streaming has started.

options.text: A `303`, so the browser follows it with a GET to `/posts`
options.why: Progressive-enhancement form posts get a 303 so the follow-up request is a GET.

explanation: In a Server Action, `redirect` does a client-side navigation when JavaScript is available. For progressive-enhancement submissions, a plain HTML form POST, it returns `303 See Other`, so the browser loads `/posts` with GET instead of re-posting the form. Outside Server Actions the default is `307`, and `308` for `permanentRedirect`.

stem: A user goes `/posts` → `/posts/new` with a `<Link>`, then submits a form whose Server Action ends with `redirect('/posts/99')`, using the default redirect type. On `/posts/99` they press the browser Back button once. Where do they land?

options.text: `/posts`, because the Server Action redirect replaced `/posts/new`
options.why: Replace is the default outside Server Actions; inside them the default is push.

options.text: `/posts/new`, because Server Action redirects push by default
options.why: The redirect added `/posts/99` as a new entry, so Back returns to the form.

options.text: The page they were on before `/posts`, since redirects reset history
options.why: Redirects don't clear history; they either push or replace one entry.

options.text: `/posts/99` again, because Back is blocked after a Server Action
options.why: There is no such blocking; Back works as usual.

explanation: `redirect(path, type)` defaults to `push` in Server Actions and to `replace` everywhere else. Here the stack becomes `/posts`, `/posts/new`, `/posts/99`, and Back shows the form again. To keep the form out of history, call `redirect('/posts/99', RedirectType.replace)`.

stem: Which of these invalidate entries in the App Router's client cache (the in-memory store of React Server Component payloads)? (Choose three.)

options.text: Calling `revalidatePath('/posts')` in a Server Action
options.why: Server-side revalidation also invalidates the related client cache entries.

options.text: Calling `cookies().set(...)` in a Server Action
options.why: Setting or deleting a cookie in an action invalidates the client cache.

options.text: Calling `router.refresh()` from a Client Component
options.why: `refresh` clears the client cache for the current route.

options.text: Calling `window.history.pushState` with a new query string
options.why: It syncs `useSearchParams` and `usePathname`; it doesn't touch the cache.

options.text: Calling `router.prefetch()` again for the same route
options.why: Prefetching fills the cache; it doesn't evict existing entries.

explanation: The glossary lists the ways to invalidate the client cache programmatically: `revalidateTag`, `revalidatePath`, `updateTag`, `router.refresh`, and `cookies.set` or `cookies.delete`. A full page refresh clears it too. History API calls only keep the router's URL hooks in sync, and prefetching adds entries rather than removing them.

stem: Using the default `staleTimes` (dynamic = 0), a user opens `/inbox`, which is dynamic, then clicks through to a message. Meanwhile a new email arrives on the server. The user presses Back. Why does the inbox still show the old list?

options.text: The dynamic page stayed cached for 30 seconds
options.why: The 30-second default ended with Next.js 15; it is now 0.

options.text: Back/forward reuses the cached page, regardless of `staleTimes`
options.why: The client cache restores it to avoid layout shift and keep scroll.

options.text: `useSearchParams` needs a `<Suspense>` boundary to refresh
options.why: Suspense boundaries are about prerendering, not back navigation.

options.text: The browser's HTTP cache served the old HTML document for `/inbox` again
options.why: This is a client-side transition; no new HTML document is loaded.

explanation: Pages aren't reused from the client cache on new navigations when `staleTimes.dynamic` is 0, but they are reused during browser back/forward navigation. `staleTimes` doesn't change that behaviour, which exists to prevent layout shift and keep scroll position. If the data must be fresh on return, refresh it explicitly, for example with `router.refresh()`, or invalidate it when the data changes.

stem: A page shows a price fetched with a `fetch` cached on the server. An admin changes the price, then calls `router.refresh()` from a Client Component. The page still shows the old price. Which statements explain this or fix it? (Choose two.)

options.text: `refresh()` re-renders, but the cached `fetch` returns its old result
options.why: Refresh doesn't invalidate server caches, so cached requests can give the same result.

options.text: A Server Action that calls `revalidateTag` or `revalidatePath` fixes it
options.why: Server-side cached data has to be invalidated on the server.

options.text: `refresh()` only re-renders Client Components, so server data can't change
options.why: Refresh makes a new server request and re-renders Server Components.

options.text: Calling `router.refresh()` twice in a row forces a cache miss
options.why: Repeating it hits the same cached data on the server.

options.text: Replacing it with `router.push` to the same URL bypasses the cache
options.why: Navigation uses the same server caches; it doesn't purge them.

explanation: `router.refresh()` clears the client cache for the current route and re-renders Server Components with a fresh request, but it does not invalidate the server-side cache. The docs warn it can return the same result if `fetch` requests are cached. Invalidate on the server with `revalidateTag`, `updateTag` or `revalidatePath`, usually in the Server Action that performs the mutation.

stem: A page wraps `const user = await getUser(id)` in `try { ... } catch (e) { console.error(e) }`, and `getUser` calls `notFound()` when no user exists. For a missing user, the route's `not-found.tsx` is still rendered.

options.text: True
options.why: `notFound()` works by throwing, so the catch block swallows it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the try/catch suppresses it, so no not-found UI renders.

explanation: `notFound()` throws a special `NEXT_HTTP_ERROR_FALLBACK;404` error that has to reach Next.js. A `try/catch` around the call swallows it, so the not-found UI never renders. Either let the error propagate, or call `unstable_rethrow(e)` at the top of the catch block so framework errors from `notFound()` and `redirect()` pass through.

stem: A product page has a `loading.tsx`. The page awaits a slow product lookup, and calls `notFound()` when the product doesn't exist. What does a crawler requesting a missing product URL receive?

options.text: An HTTP `404`, because `notFound()` always sets the response status code
options.why: The status can't change once the response headers have been sent.

options.text: An HTTP `500`, because the throw happens mid-stream
options.why: Next.js handles `notFound()`; it isn't treated as a crash.

options.text: An HTTP `200` with a `noindex` robots meta tag in the HTML
options.why: Streaming had already started, so the 404 UI comes with a `noindex` tag.

options.text: A `307` redirect to the route's `not-found` page
options.why: `notFound()` renders the not-found UI in place; it doesn't redirect.

explanation: The `loading.tsx` fallback starts streaming the response, which sends the headers with a `200` status. When `notFound()` then throws, Next.js can no longer change the status. It streams the not-found UI with `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` so the URL isn't indexed. For a real `404` status, check existence before anything suspends, for example in `proxy`, or before any `Suspense` boundary or slow `await`.

stem: A Client Component reads `useSearchParams()` to sort a product list, and a button runs `window.history.pushState(null, '', '?sort=asc')`. What happens next?

options.text: Nothing, until you also call `router.refresh()`
options.why: No extra call is needed; the router hooks pick up the change.

options.text: `useSearchParams()` returns the new value and the component re-renders
options.why: Native `pushState` integrates with the router, so its hooks stay in sync.

options.text: The browser does a full reload of `?sort=asc`
options.why: `pushState` changes the URL and history without loading a new document.

options.text: Next.js reverts the URL, because only `router.push` is allowed to change it
options.why: Next.js explicitly supports native `pushState` and `replaceState`.

explanation: Next.js lets you call `window.history.pushState` and `replaceState` directly. These calls integrate with the Next.js router, so `usePathname` and `useSearchParams` update and re-render their components without a page reload. `pushState` adds a history entry, so Back undoes the sort; `replaceState` overwrites the current entry.
reference: Next.js docs: Linking and Navigating (Native History API)

stem: Match each navigation requirement to the App Router feature that addresses it.

options.text: `onNavigate` with `e.preventDefault()` on `<Link>`
`useLinkStatus()` inside the link
`prefetch={active ? null : false}`, set on mouse enter
`window.location.href = '/login'`

prompts.text: Stop leaving a form that has unsaved edits
Show a small pending hint on the clicked link while a slow, unprefetched route loads
Prefetch only the links a user hovers over in a long list
On logout, throw away all client-side state with a full reload

explanation: `onNavigate` runs only for client-side navigations and can cancel them, which suits unsaved-changes guards. `useLinkStatus` exposes a `pending` flag to descendants of a `<Link>`. Switching `prefetch` from `false` to `null` on hover limits prefetching to links the user shows intent for. Assigning `window.location.href` forces a document load, which clears all client state; the docs recommend it for logout flows.
reference: Next.js docs: Link component; useLinkStatus; Preserving UI state

stem: A team adds `useLinkStatus()` hints to the links of a statically prerendered menu, with no `prefetch` prop. In production the pending hint almost never appears. Why?

options.text: The hook only works when called from the layout itself
options.why: It must be called inside a descendant of the `<Link>`, not in the layout.

options.text: `useLinkStatus` needs a `<Suspense>` boundary around the menu
options.why: No Suspense boundary is involved; the hook reads navigation state.

options.text: Prefetched links skip the pending state
options.why: Static routes are prefetched, so navigation is immediate and pending is skipped.

options.text: The hook always returns `{ pending: false }` in production
options.why: That happens in the Pages Router, not the App Router.

explanation: `useLinkStatus` is most useful when navigation is blocked: prefetching is disabled or still in progress, or the destination is dynamic with no `loading.js`. If a route was already prefetched, the pending state is skipped. Static routes in the viewport are prefetched in full, so users rarely see the hint. That is the intended behaviour.

stem: A `<Link href="/editor" onNavigate={...}>` guards unsaved changes. In which situations does `onNavigate` NOT run, even though the user activated a link? (Choose two.)

options.text: The user Ctrl/Cmd-clicks the link to open it in a new tab
options.why: Modifier-key clicks open a new tab, which is not a client-side navigation.

options.text: The `<Link>` points to an external URL on another origin
options.why: Only same-origin client-side navigations trigger `onNavigate`.

options.text: The user does a normal left click on a same-origin link
options.why: That is exactly the client-side navigation `onNavigate` runs for.

options.text: The destination route is dynamic and not prefetched
options.why: Prefetch state doesn't matter; it is still a client-side navigation.

options.text: The link uses the `replace` prop
options.why: `replace` changes history handling, not whether `onNavigate` runs.

explanation: `onClick` runs for every click, but `onNavigate` runs only during client-side navigation. It doesn't run for Ctrl/Cmd-clicks (new tab), external URLs, or links with a `download` attribute. An unsaved-changes guard that relies only on `onNavigate` therefore won't catch every way of leaving the page; tab closes and reloads need a `beforeunload` listener as well.

stem: Which statements about `useSelectedLayoutSegments()` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: The returned segments include route groups such as `(marketing)`
options.why: The docs suggest filtering out entries that start with a bracket.

options.text: A catch-all match is returned as one joined string in the array
options.why: `/blog/a/b/c` from `app/blog/layout` gives `['a/b/c']`.

options.text: It returns every segment from the root, whichever layout calls it
options.why: It returns the active segments below the calling layout only.

options.text: It returns `null` when no child segment is active
options.why: It returns an empty array; `useSelectedLayoutSegment` is the one that returns `null`.

options.text: It can be called directly inside a Server Component layout
options.why: It is a Client Component hook, used from a component that the layout imports.

explanation: `useSelectedLayoutSegments` returns an array of the active segments below the layout it is called from, or `[]`. Route groups appear in the array, which breadcrumb UIs usually filter out. Catch-all segments are joined into a single string. Like its singular sibling, it is a Client Component hook.

stem: The route `app/blog/[...slug]/page.tsx` is visited at `/blog/2024/06/launch`. A Client Component imported into the root `app/layout.tsx` calls `useSelectedLayoutSegments()`. How many elements does the returned array have? Type a number.
explanation: Called from the root layout, the hook returns the segments below it: `'blog'`, plus the catch-all match. All matched catch-all segments are joined into one string, so the result is `['blog', '2024/06/launch']`, which has 2 elements.

stem: `proxy.ts` rewrites `/dashboard` to `/auth/dashboard` for signed-in users and to `/public/dashboard` for everyone else. How should a `<Link>` to the dashboard be written so it prefetches the right page while the address bar shows `/dashboard`?

options.text: `<Link href="/dashboard" prefetch>`, and let the proxy resolve the rewrite on each prefetch
options.why: That needs extra proxy round trips to work out which route to prefetch.

options.text: `<Link as="/dashboard" href={isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'}>`
options.why: `href` names the real route to prefetch, and `as` is the URL that's shown.

options.text: `<Link href="/auth/dashboard" replace>` for every user
options.why: It would prefetch and show the wrong page to visitors who aren't signed in.

options.text: `<Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>`
options.why: That avoids the problem by giving up prefetching altogether.

explanation: When proxy rewrites a URL to different routes, `<Link>` can't tell which one to prefetch without asking the proxy. The docs recommend passing the real destination as `href`, computed from client-side auth state, and the displayed URL as `as`. Prefetching then targets the correct page with no extra proxy work.
reference: Next.js docs: Link component (Prefetching links in Proxy)

stem: Without Cache Components, `app/account/layout.tsx` awaits `cookies()` and an uncached `fetch` for the user. `app/account/loading.tsx` exists. Navigating to `/account` still freezes for about a second before anything changes. Why?

options.text: `loading.tsx` is only shown on the first, server-rendered visit
options.why: It is prefetched and used on client navigations too.

options.text: `loading.tsx` wraps the page but not the layout, so the layout blocks
options.why: Runtime data in the same segment's layout blocks until it finishes rendering.

options.text: `cookies()` turns off client-side transitions for the route
options.why: Transitions still happen; the delay comes from the layout rendering.

options.text: `loading.tsx` must be marked as a Client Component to show during navigation
options.why: It is a Server Component by default and works as one.

explanation: `loading.js` wraps `page.js`, nested layouts and `not-found.js` in a `<Suspense>` boundary, but not the `layout.js` in the same segment. When that layout reads runtime or uncached data, navigation waits for the layout to render, so the skeleton can't show. Move the data fetching into `page.tsx`, or wrap the runtime-data part of the layout in its own `<Suspense>`.

stem: A dynamic `/orders` page shows live order statuses. To make navigation feel instant, a developer changes its nav link to `<Link href="/orders" prefetch={true}>`, and keeps the default `staleTimes`. What new problem can this cause?

options.text: None: dynamic pages are never reused from the client cache
options.why: That holds for the `dynamic` period, but full prefetches use the `static` period.

options.text: Each click now forces a fresh server render
options.why: Click navigations reuse the prefetched entry; they don't force a re-render.

options.text: The build fails, because `prefetch={true}` needs a static route
options.why: Full prefetching is allowed for dynamic routes.

options.text: Clicks within about 5 minutes can show a stale prefetched list
options.why: `prefetch={true}` entries use `staleTimes.static`, which defaults to 5 minutes.

explanation: The `staleTimes.static` lifetime, 5 minutes by default, applies to static pages, to `<Link prefetch={true}>` and to `router.prefetch()`. The `dynamic` lifetime, 0 by default, applies only to pages that are neither static nor fully prefetched. A full prefetch of a live page can therefore be reused for minutes. Keep the default prefetch and use `loading.tsx`, lower `staleTimes.static`, or invalidate after relevant mutations.

stem: With `cacheComponents: true`, which statements describe how the App Router preserves UI state across navigations? (Choose three.)

options.text: Pages are hidden with React `<Activity>`, so their DOM and state survive
options.why: Hidden pages stay in the document with `display: none`, keeping their state.

options.text: Up to 3 routes are kept; older ones re-render fresh when you return
options.why: Beyond 3 routes, the oldest is evicted.

options.text: `router.bfcacheId` changes on push or replace, but not on back/forward
options.why: Using it as a `key` resets state on fresh navigations and keeps it on Back.

options.text: Every visited route stays mounted until a full page reload
options.why: Only up to 3 routes are preserved, not all of them.

options.text: `router.bfcacheId` changes after every `router.refresh()`
options.why: It stays the same for refreshes and for search-param or hash-only changes.

explanation: With Cache Components, the router hides pages with `<Activity>` instead of unmounting them, so form drafts, scroll positions and open `<details>` survive. Up to 3 routes are preserved. `bfcacheId` changes when a push or replace navigation creates the segment fresh, but not for back/forward, `refresh()`, or search-param and hash-only changes. The docs suggest using it as a React key mainly while migrating.
reference: Next.js docs: Preserving UI state; useRouter (bfcacheId)

stem: With Cache Components on, a settings page opens a dialog with `useState(false)`, and a `useEffect` keyed on `isDialogOpen` focuses its input. A user navigates away while the dialog is open, comes back, and clicks Edit, which calls `setIsDialogOpen(true)`. The input is not focused. Which fix does the Next.js guide recommend?

options.text: Add `prefetch={false}` to links that lead back to the page
options.why: Prefetching doesn't cause this; state preservation does.

options.text: Set `staleTimes.static` to 0 so the page re-renders on return
options.why: Client-cache lifetimes don't reset state that `<Activity>` preserved.

options.text: Derive the open state from a search param, not `useState`
options.why: Leaving changes the URL, so returning starts closed and opening changes state again.

options.text: Replace `useEffect` with `useMemo` so the focus logic runs on every render
options.why: `useMemo` is not for side effects such as focusing.

explanation: `<Activity>` kept `isDialogOpen` as `true` while the page was hidden. Clicking Edit sets it to `true` again, which is no state change, so the focus effect doesn't re-run. The guide's fix is to derive the dialog's state from the URL, for example `?dialog=open`. Navigating away clears the param, so on return the dialog starts closed, and opening it changes the derived state and triggers the effect.
reference: Next.js docs: Preserving UI state (Dialog and initialization logic)

stem: With Cache Components on, user A writes a draft in a `useState`-backed form, logs out (`await signOut(); router.push('/login')`), and user B signs in on the same browser. User B opens the compose page and sees A's draft. What is the most robust fix for the logout flow?

options.text: Call `router.refresh()` right after `router.push('/login')` to reset the page
options.why: A refresh re-renders server output but keeps client state.

options.text: Clear the draft in the `/login` page's `useEffect`
options.why: The login page can't reach state held by a hidden, preserved page.

options.text: Lower `staleTimes.dynamic` so the compose page re-renders
options.why: Client-cache lifetimes don't clear React state preserved by `<Activity>`.

options.text: Navigate with `window.location.href = '/login'` to force a full reload
options.why: A document reload discards all client-side state, including preserved pages.

explanation: `<Activity>` preserves local component state across navigations, auth changes included: new props cause a re-render but don't reset existing state. The docs recommend `window.location.href` for logout so the page reloads and every preserved page is thrown away. For narrower resets without a reload, key components on the user ID, for example `<Form key={userId} />`.
reference: Next.js docs: Preserving UI state (State and authentication)

stem: A Server Action creates an invoice and should land the user on the invoice list with the new row visible. JavaScript is loaded. Put these steps in the order they run.

options.text: The action validates the form data and writes the invoice to the database
The action calls `revalidatePath('/invoices')`
The action calls `redirect('/invoices')`, which throws and ends the action
The client performs a client-side navigation to `/invoices`
`/invoices` renders with fresh data that includes the new invoice

explanation: Mutate first, then invalidate, then redirect. `revalidatePath` must come before `redirect` because `redirect` throws and nothing after it runs. With JavaScript available, the redirect from a Server Action becomes a client-side navigation rather than an HTTP 303. The destination renders from the invalidated cache, so it includes the new row.

options.text: `revalidatePath` throws when it is called inside a `try` block
options.why: `revalidatePath` doesn't throw here; the throwing call is `redirect`.

options.text: The database write succeeds only after the response has been sent
options.why: The write is awaited before anything else runs.

options.text: `redirect` can't be used in actions called through `useActionState`
options.why: `redirect` is supported there; it just has to escape the `try`.

options.text: The catch swallows the error that `redirect` throws to navigate
options.why: `redirect` throws `NEXT_REDIRECT`; caught here, it becomes an error message.

explanation: `redirect()` works by throwing a `NEXT_REDIRECT` error that Next.js must receive. Inside the `try`, the `catch` takes it, logs it and returns an error state, even though the write and the revalidation already succeeded. Call `redirect` after the `try/catch`, or call `unstable_rethrow(e)` first in the catch block so framework errors propagate.

stem: A statically prerendered page is served at `/promo` through a `proxy.ts` rewrite from `/landing`. Its header shows the active path with `usePathname()`, and production logs a hydration mismatch on that text. Which approach do the docs suggest?

options.text: Read `window.location.pathname` during render instead
options.why: That runs on the client only, so the server HTML still won't match.

options.text: Add `suppressHydrationWarning` to the root `<html>` element to silence the error
options.why: That flag silences one element's text or attributes, not a nested header.

options.text: Render a stable fallback, and set the client path in an effect after mount
options.why: The server and first client render agree, and the real path appears after hydration.

options.text: Move `usePathname()` into a Server Component
options.why: Reading the URL in a Server Component isn't supported.

explanation: A prerendered page's HTML is built for its source path. When proxy or `next.config` rewrites serve it under another URL, `usePathname()` on the client returns a different value, which causes a hydration mismatch. The docs recommend isolating the part that depends on the path: render a stable fallback on the server, and copy `usePathname()` into state in a `useEffect` after mount.
reference: Next.js docs: usePathname (Avoid hydration mismatch with rewrites)

stem: With `cacheComponents: true`, the shared `app/docs/layout.tsx` renders a sidebar Client Component that calls `usePathname()` to highlight the active link. `app/docs/[slug]/page.tsx` has no `generateStaticParams`, and `next build` fails. Which changes fix the build? (Choose two.)

options.text: Wrap the sidebar, or a parent, in `<Suspense>` with a fallback
options.why: A suspending `usePathname` needs a boundary so its fallback can prerender.

options.text: Add `generateStaticParams` that returns every `slug`
options.why: With every param known at build time, the pathname resolves while prerendering.

options.text: Add `'use client'` to `app/docs/layout.tsx`
options.why: The hook still suspends on unknown params, wherever the client boundary is.

options.text: Read `window.location.pathname` in the sidebar during render
options.why: There is no `window` during prerendering, and it would break hydration.

options.text: Call `usePathname()` from inside a `useEffect`
options.why: Hooks can't be called inside effects; that breaks the rules of hooks.

explanation: With Cache Components, `usePathname` (and `useParams`, `useSelectedLayoutSegment(s)`) suspends when the route has a dynamic param that `generateStaticParams` doesn't cover, because the pathname isn't known until request time. This applies even to a static component in a layout. Either give it a `<Suspense>` boundary, so the rest of the layout still prerenders, or make every param known at build time.

stem:
A product listing page shows 50 `<Link>` cards. Analytics shows "product viewed" events for products users never opened. The detail pages log the view in a Server Component like this:

```tsx
export default async function Product({ params }) {
  const { id } = await params
  await trackView(id)
  return <ProductView id={id} />
}
```

What is happening, and what is the fix?

options.text: Search crawlers request each URL; block them in `robots.txt`
options.why: It happens in real sessions, as soon as cards scroll into view.

options.text: Prefetching renders the page; log the view from an effect or Server Action
options.why: Side effects in render run on prefetch, so move them to a user-driven trigger.

options.text: `await params` re-runs the page component once for every card shown on the list
options.why: Each card is a link, not an instance of the page component.

options.text: React StrictMode double-renders the page in production
options.why: StrictMode double rendering only happens in development.

explanation: Layouts and pages must be pure. When a `<Link>` enters the viewport, Next.js may prefetch, and so render, its route before anyone clicks. A side effect such as analytics in the page body then fires on prefetch. The prefetching guide recommends moving such effects into a `useEffect` or a Server Action called from a Client Component, so they run only when the page is actually shown.

stem: A Client Component calls `router.push(url)`, where `url` comes from a `?next=` query parameter so users return to where they started. What is the danger?

options.text: `router.push` can't navigate to paths that have query strings
options.why: Query strings are fully supported in `router.push`.

options.text: Pushing to a same-origin URL makes the browser reload the whole page
options.why: `router.push` performs a client-side transition.

options.text: The query value is URL-decoded twice, so the redirect breaks
options.why: Next.js doesn't double-decode it.

options.text: A crafted `javascript:` URL can run script in your page (XSS)
options.why: The docs warn against passing untrusted URLs to `push` or `replace`.

explanation: The `useRouter` docs warn that untrusted or unsanitized URLs must not be passed to `router.push` or `router.replace`: a `javascript:` URL is executed in the page's context, which is cross-site scripting. Validate `next` against an allow-list or require a same-origin relative path, for example check that it starts with `/` but not `//`, before navigating.

stem: Setting `experimental.staleTimes = { dynamic: 0, static: 0 }` makes browser Back and Forward navigations always fetch a fresh page from the server.

options.text: True
options.why: Back/forward caching is a separate behaviour that `staleTimes` doesn't affect.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `staleTimes` leaves back/forward caching unchanged.

explanation: The `staleTimes` reference says it doesn't change back/forward caching, which exists to prevent layout shift and keep scroll position. Back and Forward reuse cached entries for visited pages whatever `staleTimes` says. To get fresh data after returning, refresh explicitly, or invalidate when the data changes.
